summary:
Ekiti State stands under Nigeria's uniform national criminalisation framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches far beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states; the same advice notes that the same-sex marriage law reaches those who help arrange or attend such weddings.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case surfaced in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Ekiti State itself has documented trans-specific violence. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report records that on 21 January 2014, days after the SSMPA was passed, Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman, was beaten by six men in Ado Ekiti, the state capital, who threatened 'You will get 14 years in prison!'; the report states she was beaten at least twice over the period and, unable to use Ekiti health services safely, travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment.

Arrest and extortion are established patterns in Ado Ekiti. The same Human Rights Watch report records a September 2014 arrest at Faguyi bar in Ado Ekiti of a gay man on his third arrest, released after two days in detention after paying 2,000 Naira for himself and 10,000 Naira for a friend, and a 2014 incident in which a 25-year-old gay man was extorted by a state investigator in Ado Ekiti.
tangentialFactors:
The SSMPA's reach extends to third parties: the UK FCDO's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns that the same-sex marriage law criminalises those who help arrange or attend such weddings, not only the parties.

Enforcement in Ekiti State has historically combined formal arrest with informal extraction. The Human Rights Watch (October 2016) documentation of the Faguyi bar arrest and the state investigator's extortion shows detention used as a revenue mechanism rather than a prosecution pathway.

Healthcare access is a compounding risk for trans visitors in Ekiti. Debbie's case shows that fear of being identified at state health facilities pushed her to travel three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment, a pattern that would affect any trans visitor needing routine or emergency care in Ado Ekiti.

Comparatively, Ekiti State's enforcement sits within the southern secular-law regime rather than the northern Sharia zone where male sodomy can carry the death penalty; the twelve northern states represent a materially different risk tier for trans and gender-nonconforming visitors.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ekiti State live under the same national SSMPA framework as visitors, but with the added exposure of routine local police contact. Human Rights Watch documents repeated arrests of gay men in Ado Ekiti, including one man arrested three times by September 2014, and a 2014 incident in which a state investigator extorted a 25-year-old gay man.

Trans residents face both community violence and healthcare avoidance. Debbie, a 26-year-old transgender woman in Ado Ekiti, was beaten at least twice in the period following the SSMPA's passage, the first incident on 21 January 2014 involving six men who threatened her with the 14-year penalty; she avoided Ekiti health services and travelled three hours each way to Ibadan for HIV treatment.

Nationally, trans Nigerians face lethal violence with limited accountability. The August 2024 killing of the transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama in Abuja saw police describe the victim as a man in female clothing, and The Dial (February 2025) records that no suspects had been charged six months later.

Bobrisky's 2024 imprisonment shows that placement of trans women in male or female prison sections is left to official discretion; an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act for a first-time offender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have since been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The sources do not resolve how Ekiti State authorities would currently assign housing for a detained trans woman, or whether any state-level guidance exists beyond the discretionary pattern visible in the Bobrisky case.

No source in this inventory documents a specific Ekiti State enforcement action against a trans person after 2014; the Ado Ekiti incidents recorded by Human Rights Watch are from 2014 and their current representativeness is not sourced.
